articles.title: Psychology’s tools for measuring masculinity lean heavily toward the negative, review finds
articles.summary: Is psychology only looking for problems when it studies men? A review of 50 years of masculinity scales found that 78 percent focused mainly on harms, and many overlooked culture and social context.

articles.title: Scientists uncover an intriguing link between your metabolism and your sense of time
articles.summary: How quickly time seems to pass may be linked to how much energy your body burns at rest, your stress chemistry, and your working memory, according to a new study.

articles.title: Don't Blame The Preferences: Examining The Emergence of Sycophancy in LLM Training
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI sycophancy, the tendency of large language models (LLMs) to flatter users and affirm their beliefs, can undermine accuracy and contribute to misinformation, dependence, and overconfidence. Although prior work has benchmarked sycophancy in released models and proposed mitigations, its origins during training remain poorly understood. Preference alignment methods such as RLHF and DPO are often blamed, but their effects are rarely compared with earlier training stages. articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable approach for annotating mental health and crisis-related social media content, but their reliability in safety-critical tasks remains unclear. articles.title: How interpreting a racing heart relates to sexual functioning in men and women
articles.summary: A recent study shows that interpreting physical signs like a racing heart as exciting is linked to higher sexual desire, while fearing those same physical sensations relates to sexual dissatisfaction and physical difficulties.

articles.title: The link between genes and kids’ IQ shifts as they grow up, large study finds
articles.summary: As children grow from age 4 to 16, the link between common education-related genetic variants and IQ strengthens, while the link between rare damaging mutations and lower IQ weakens, according to a study of British children.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
articles.summary: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.
